items.title: American Security Robotics Act of 2026

committee.H.R. 8189: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
committee.S. 4235: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs

items.status: H.R. 8189: 2026-04-02 — Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.; S. 4235: 2026-03-26 — Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
items.summary: Bars executive agencies from procuring covered unmanned ground vehicle systems made or assembled by covered foreign entities. After one year, bars agency operation and use of federal funds through contracts, grants, cooperative agreements, or otherwise for procurement or operation. The definition explicitly includes ground mobile robotics, autonomous patrol technology, and humanoid robots.
items.mechanism_scope_limitations: Applies to federal executive agencies and systems manufactured or assembled by entities domiciled in or controlled by a covered nation, or their subsidiaries/affiliates. DHS, DOD, State, and DOJ receive an exemption only for specified national-interest uses (research/testing/training/electronic or information warfare/counterterrorism etc.) or systems modified so they cannot exchange data with covered foreign entities and pose no agency-determined cybersecurity risk. It does not create a general private-sector ban.

quotes.quote: Except as provided under subsection (e), the head of an executive agency may not procure any covered unmanned ground vehicle system.
beginning on the date that is one year after the date of the enactment of this Act, no executive agency may operate a covered unmanned ground vehicle system.

latest_actions.text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

items.title: National Commission on Robotics Act

sponsor.H.R. 7334: Rep. Jay Obernolte (introduced for himself, Rep. Jennifer McClellan, and Rep. Robert Latta)
sponsor.S. 4686: Sen. Dave McCormick (introduced for himself, Sens. John Hickenlooper, Todd Young, and Martin Heinrich)

committee.H.R. 7334: House Committees on Science, Space, and Technology; Energy and Commerce; Foreign Affairs; and Education and Workforce
committee.S. 4686: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

items.status: H.R. 7334: 2026-02-03 — Referred to the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, and in addition to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Foreign Affairs, and Education and Workforce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.; S. 4686: 2026-06-04 — Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
items.summary: Establishes an independent robotics commission to review advances in robotics and recommend policies addressing U.S. economic competitiveness and national security. Its review includes domestic and international competitiveness, strategic investment and partnerships, workforce, supply chains, and manufacturing. It requires an interim report within one year and a final report within two years after the commission is established, then terminates the commission 18 months after the final report.
items.mechanism_scope_limitations: Creates a time-limited advisory commission, not an operating robotics agency or direct regulatory regime. The House and Senate bills are substantially parallel in purpose and review/report structure, with differences in some provisions and text; this record does not treat one as a formal companion unless Congress.gov explicitly labels them so.

quotes.quote: The Commission shall carry out a review of advances in robotics.

Not later than two years after the date on which the Commission is established under subsection (a), the Commission shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees and the President a final report

unresolved_discrepancies: H.R. 7334 and S. 4686 share the title and substantially similar structure, but the bills are independently introduced and their texts contain differences; exact companion/identical-bill status was not verified from a Congress.gov relationship record.

latest_actions.text: Referred to the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, and in addition to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Foreign Affairs, and Education and Workforce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

items.title: Humanoid Robotics Oversight and Blocking of Obtainment from Totalitarians Act of 2025 (Humanoid ROBOT Act of 2025)
items.sponsor: Sen. Bill Cassidy (introduced for himself and Sen. Chris Coons)
items.committee: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
items.status: S. 3275: 2025-11-20 — Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
items.summary: Bars executive agency procurement or use by federal contractors of humanoid robots designed, tested, developed, or manufactured by covered entities, with a Defense Secretary waiver for national-security or research objectives. Directs CFIUS to review certain investments in humanoid-robot production. Directs the Defense Secretary to report within a year on national-security threats, including privacy/data security, supply-side development and export-control or IP concerns.
items.mechanism_scope_limitations: Procurement/contractor prohibitions apply 180 days after enactment; the waiver is assigned to the Secretary of Defense. The CFIUS review and DoD report concern countries/entities defined in the bill; this is a federal procurement, investment-review, and reporting framework rather than a general civilian use prohibition.

quotes.quote: A person awarded a contract by an executive agency may not use a humanoid robot designed, tested, developed, or manufactured by a covered entity to fulfill, execute, or otherwise support carrying out the contract.

latest_actions.text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

items.title: Blocking CCP Spy Tech Act of 2026

sponsor.S. 4586: Sen. Rick Scott (introduced for himself and Sen. Tom Cotton)

committee.H.R. 9687: House Committees on Energy and Commerce and Armed Services

items.status: H.R. 9687: 2026-07-14 — Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Armed Services, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.; S. 4586: 2026-05-20 — Read twice and referred to the Select Committee on Intelligence.
items.summary: Requires an appropriate national-security agency to assess within one year whether communications equipment or services produced/provided by six named entities and their specified affiliates, joint ventures, or licensees pose an unacceptable national-security or U.S.-person safety/security risk. A positive determination triggers FCC addition to its covered list; if the agency misses the deadline, the FCC must add all listed entities’ covered products/services. A negative determination triggers reporting and follow-on review by other national-security agencies. Both introduced versions also direct the Defense Secretary to determine whether named entities should be identified as Chinese military companies under the annual NDAA review.
items.mechanism_scope_limitations: The House text names Game Science, DeepSeek, Unitree Robotics, DEEP Robotics, BrainCo, and Manycore Tech, and defined related entities. The Senate bill has the same short title and central review/list mechanism; both introduced texts include a DoD Chinese-military-company determination section. The core effect is risk assessment and possible FCC covered-list restrictions, not a general private possession ban.

quotes.quote: If an appropriate national security agency does not make a determination as required by subsection (a), the Commission shall, not later than 30 days after the date specified in subsection (a), add all communications equipment and services described in subsection (b) to the covered list.

the Secretary of Defense shall determine if any entity described in section 2(b) should be identified under such section 1260H(a) as a Chinese military company operating directly or indirectly in the United States.

latest_actions.text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Armed Services, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

items.title: Guarding the U.S. against Adversarial Robotics Dominance Act of 2026 (GUARD Act of 2026)
items.sponsor: Rep. John R. Moolenaar (introduced for himself, Rep. Jay Obernolte, and Rep. Jennifer McClellan)
items.committee: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
items.status: H.R. 9129: 2026-09-01 — Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.
items.summary: Directs an appropriate national-security agency to determine within one year whether covered humanoid/quadruped robotics communications equipment or services pose an unacceptable risk to U.S. national security or the safety/security of U.S. persons. If the agency does not make a determination by the deadline, the FCC must add all covered equipment/services to its covered list; affirmative findings trigger listing and reporting. A negative finding requires reporting and review by other appropriate national-security agencies.
items.mechanism_scope_limitations: Covers humanoid or quadruped ground robots, their control software/external devices, when they are communications equipment or services produced/provided by a covered foreign entity (including entities tied to a country of concern through control, ownership, joint venture, or technology-sharing/licensing). The bill provides a path to avoid listing on a timely negative determination; it does not itself impose a direct across-the-board procurement or private ownership ban.

quotes.quote: If the appropriate national security agency does not make a determination as required by paragraph (1) within 1 year after the enactment of this Act, the Commission shall add all covered robotics communications equipment or services to the covered list.
H.R. 9129, H.R. 6152, H.R. 2805, and H.R. 4950 were forwarded to the full Committee, without amendment.
quotes.reference: Congressional Record, Daily Digest, 2026-09-01, House subcommittee markup entry

latest_actions.text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.

items.title: Prohibition on Chinese Humanoid Robotic Systems (FY2027 NDAA markup item)
items.summary: Gooden’s markup log item 6312, revision 2, was agreed to by voice vote. The House-passed FY2027 NDAA contains a related Section 163 barring DoD procurement, leasing or obtaining of covered humanoid robotic systems made or developed by foreign adversaries, or carrying their software, AI, cloud or remote-control services. A controlled-testing waiver and exclusions for fixed industrial robots, non-networked systems and regulated medical devices apply.
items.mechanism_scope_limitations: Section 163 applies to contracts and agreements after enactment and requires implementation guidance within 180 days. It is not a general civilian possession ban. The markup log identifies Gooden’s contribution but does not independently prove verbatim continuity into Section 163; the House-passed text establishes that section’s scope. House passage is not enactment.

quotes.quote: The Secretary of Defense may not procure, lease, or otherwise obtain a covered humanoid robotic system

unresolved_discrepancies: Exact amendment-to-section lineage not independently established; related operative text verified in House-passed §163.

items.title: Outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan for National Economic and Social Development
items.institution: National People’s Congress; outline republished by Beijing Municipal People’s Congress
items.summary: The 2026–2030 outline places robotics among strategic emerging industries and embodied intelligence among future industries. It directs AI-plus adoption, model/algorithm work including embodied AI, and real-world application pilots; the text is a broad planning framework rather than an appropriated robotics program.
items.mechanism: Five-year national guidance: industrial prioritization, application demonstrations, future-industry pilots, and AI+ deployment.
items.limitations: The plan names eight strategic emerging industries and six future-industry fields across the relevant clauses; it does not establish an official “10 industry tracks” count. No robotics-specific quantified national target in the plan text located.

exact_quotes.quote: 推动量子科技、生物制造、氢能和核聚变能、脑机接口、具身智能、第六代移动通信等成为新的经济增长点。
加快新一代信息技术、新能源、新材料、智能网联新能源汽车、机器人、生物医药、高端装备、航空航天等战略性新兴产业发展

items.title: Legislative Hearing on Protecting Communications Networks and Improving Connectivity
items.institution: House Committee on Energy and Commerce, Subcommittee on Communications and Technology
items.summary: The subcommittee considered several communications bills, including H.R. 9129 (GUARD Act), which would direct scrutiny of foreign adversary robotics. Four witnesses were listed; AUVSI’s Michael Robbins was the robotics-relevant witness.

items.title: FCC Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau Announces Addition of Foreign-Produced Power Inverters and Advanced Robotic Devices to FCC Covered List
items.summary: FCC added foreign-produced advanced robotic devices to its Covered List, except devices receiving DoW Conditional Approval. It relied on an Executive Branch interagency National Security Determination that such devices posed unacceptable national-security and U.S.-person safety/security risks.
items.mechanism: Secure Networks Act Section 2 / FCC equipment-authorization and subsidy restrictions, based on the Executive Branch interagency determination attached as Appendix C to DA 26-786. Covered devices include network-capable mobile ground robots; exclusions and Department of War conditional approval matter.
items.limitations: This is a device-category supply-chain/equipment authorization mechanism; it is separate from Commerce Section 232 import investigation. The September 2026 FCC notice later describes conditional approvals.

exact_quotes.quote: Foreign-produced advanced robotic devices, except advanced robotic devices which have been granted a Conditional Approval by DoW
pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States and to the safety and security of U.S. persons

items.title: Notice of Request for Public Comments on Section 232 National Security Investigation of Imports of Robotics and Industrial Machinery
items.institution: U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security
items.summary: Commerce initiated a Section 232 investigation into national-security effects of imports of robotics and industrial machinery, parts and components. BIS requested public comments on domestic production, supply concentration, subsidies, import reliance, tariffs/quotas, employment and security risks.
items.mechanism: Trade Expansion Act Section 232 investigation under 19 U.S.C. §1862; distinct trade/import review potentially informing trade measures.
items.limitations: This is not the FCC Covered List action and does not itself establish the July 2026 foreign-produced advanced-device FCC restriction. Scope includes industrial machinery; excludes UAS.

exact_quotes.quote: On September 2, 2025, the Secretary of Commerce initiated an investigation under Section 232 (19 U.S.C. 1862)
